lead: A lag-lead compensator is two first-order sections in cascade. The lag section raises low-frequency gain, so steady-state error falls. The lead section adds positive phase near gain crossover, so phase margin and speed rise. One section alone often cannot do both jobs without hurting the other. You meet the idea in motor drives, process loops and power converters, where a plant is slow and also has large steady-state error. The design rule is simple: set the lag first, then the lead, and keep their frequency ranges apart.
prereq: You need: Chapter 5.4 for lead phase and Chapter 5.5 for lag gain, plus Bode plots from Unit 4.

blocks.text: A lag-lead compensator puts a lag section and a lead section in cascade. The lag section lifts low-frequency gain, so steady-state error falls. The lead section adds positive phase near crossover, so phase margin rises. One section alone often cannot meet both the error and the margin specification.

blocks.where: C(s) is the compensator transfer function; s is the Laplace variable, and on the Bode plot s = jω with ω the frequency in rad/s; K<sub>c</sub> is the gain constant; z<sub>1</sub> and p<sub>1</sub> are the lead zero and pole in rad/s with p<sub>1</sub> > z<sub>1</sub>; z<sub>2</sub> and p<sub>2</sub> are the lag zero and pole in rad/s with z<sub>2</sub> > p<sub>2</sub>.

items: Lead bracket: DC gain z<sub>1</sub>/p<sub>1</sub> < 1, because p<sub>1</sub> > z<sub>1</sub>; the gain rises towards 1 as frequency goes high. Maximum phase boost is near √(z<sub>1</sub>p<sub>1</sub>).
Lag bracket: DC gain z<sub>2</sub>/p<sub>2</sub> > 1, falling to 1 at high frequency.
Product DC gain: (z<sub>1</sub>/p<sub>1</sub>)(z<sub>2</sub>/p<sub>2</sub>); K<sub>c</sub> sets the absolute level.
High-frequency limit: each bracket → 1, so the product → 1.

blocks.text: The order of the two brackets does not matter; the product is the same. The block diagram shows the lag section first only by convention.

sections.h3: Bode design: lag first, lead second

blocks.text: Bode design uses gain margin, phase margin and steady-state error. The lag section is set at low frequency; the lead section is set near crossover. Keep the two frequency bands about one decade apart.

items: Find the low-frequency gain factor β > 1 needed from the steady-state error specification. The lag bracket supplies this boost.
Place the lag zero at ω<sub>z2</sub> ≈ 0.1ω<sub>c</sub>, one decade below the intended gain crossover. Place the lag pole at ω<sub>p2</sub> = ω<sub>z2</sub>/β.

The lag bracket supplies the low-frequency boost β; K<sub>c</sub> only scales the whole compensator. Set K<sub>c</sub> = (required error-constant gain)/(plant DC gain × β). Raising K<sub>c</sub> a second time to meet the error constant makes the low-frequency gain β times too large.
Add the lead zero below the new crossover and the lead pole above it. Choose the pole-zero spacing so the lead phase lifts the phase margin to the target.
Check the Bode plot. If phase margin or crossover moves too far, shift the lead pair and repeat.

blocks.text: The lead maximum phase is φ<sub>max</sub> = sin<sup>−1</sup>((α−1)/(α+1)), where α = p<sub>1</sub>/z<sub>1</sub> > 1.

Root-locus design starts from a desired dominant closed-loop pole. Place the lag pair near the origin. The lag pole p<sub>2</sub> sits closer to the origin than the lag zero z<sub>2</sub>. This pair adds only a small angle at the desired poles but raises low-frequency gain. Place the lead zero z<sub>1</sub> near the desired pole direction; place the lead pole p<sub>1</sub> farther left so the angle condition is met. The magnitude condition then gives K<sub>c</sub>. Keep lag and lead corner frequencies separated by about a decade; otherwise the lag phase cancels the lead phase at the desired pole.

figure.caption: The error enters the lag section first, then the lead section, then the plant. The lag sets low-frequency gain; the lead adds phase near crossover.

spec.aria: An error signal passes through a lag section then a lead section then the plant.

examples.question: A lag-lead compensator has lead zero 2 rad/s, lead pole 8 rad/s, lag zero 0.2 rad/s and lag pole 0.02 rad/s. Find the DC gain of the bracket product, its high-frequency limit, the phase at 4 rad/s, and K<sub>c</sub> for an overall DC gain of 1.
steps: Write C(s) = K<sub>c</sub> (s+2)/(s+8) × (s+0.2)/(s+0.02). The corner frequencies are 2, 8, 0.2 and 0.02 rad/s.
High-frequency limit: each bracket tends to 1, so the product tends to 1 × 1 = 1.
Total phase = 36.87° − 2.57° = 34.30° ≈ 34.3°. For overall DC gain 1, K<sub>c</sub> × 2.5 = 1, so K<sub>c</sub> = 0.4. With this K<sub>c</sub>, the high-frequency gain is 0.4.
examples.answer: The bracket product has DC gain 2.5, high-frequency limit 1, phase 34.3° at 4 rad/s, and K<sub>c</sub> = 0.4 for an overall DC gain of 1.
examples.check:
import math
z1, p1 = 2.0, 8.0
z2, p2 = 0.2, 0.02
w = 4.0
dc = (z1/p1)*(z2/p2)
hf = 1.0
phase = math.degrees(math.atan(w/z1) - math.atan(w/p1) + math.atan(w/z2) - math.atan(w/p2))
kc = 1.0/dc
print(dc)
print(hf)
print(round(phase, 1))
print(kc)

traps: Designing lead and lag at the same corner frequency: their phases add with opposite signs and cancel. Separate the bands by about a decade.

Forgetting K<sub>c</sub> in the DC gain: the bracket product has its own DC gain (z<sub>1</sub>/p<sub>1</sub>)(z<sub>2</sub>/p<sub>2</sub>); K<sub>c</sub> must divide it to meet the specified overall DC gain.
Placing the lag zero below its pole: for a lag section z<sub>2</sub> > p<sub>2</sub>. If you reverse them you get a lead section and the steady-state gain falls.
Using the high-frequency limit as the DC gain: each bracket tends to 1 at high frequency, so the product tends to 1; the DC value is z<sub>1</sub>z<sub>2</sub>/(p<sub>1</sub>p<sub>2</sub>).
Adding lead phase without rechecking crossover: lead raises crossover, which changes the phase of both sections; always re-evaluate phase margin.
Counting the lag boost β twice: the lag bracket already gives the low-frequency boost, so K<sub>c</sub> must not be raised again to meet the same error constant.

quiz.q: State the pole-zero condition for a lead section and for a lag section.
quiz.a: Lead: p<sub>1</sub> > z<sub>1</sub>. Lag: z<sub>2</sub> > p<sub>2</sub>. The symbols are corner frequencies in rad/s.

quiz.q: Why should the lag and lead corner frequencies be separated by about a decade?
quiz.a: So the lag phase at crossover stays small and does not cancel the lead phase. The lag then changes gain without spoiling phase margin.

quiz.q: For z<sub>1</sub> = 2 rad/s, p<sub>1</sub> = 8 rad/s, z<sub>2</sub> = 0.2 rad/s and p<sub>2</sub> = 0.02 rad/s, find the DC gain of the bracket product.
A student puts both lag corners and both lead corners at 4 rad/s. What is the net phase at 4 rad/s?
quiz.a: Each pair has zero phase separation, so the net phase is 0°. The sections cancel and no phase margin is added.

quiz.q: What does K<sub>c</sub> set in the lag-lead compensator?
quiz.a: K<sub>c</sub> sets the overall gain level; it does not change the corner frequencies.

quiz.q: The bracket product has DC gain 2.5. Find K<sub>c</sub> for an overall DC gain of 1.
In Bode design, which section is designed first and why?
quiz.a: Design the lag first to meet the steady-state error and low-frequency gain. Then design the lead to restore phase margin near crossover.

quiz.q: A plant has DC gain 2 and needs a low-frequency gain of 40 to meet its error constant. The lag section is built with β = 10. Find K<sub>c</sub> and say what goes wrong if K<sub>c</sub> is instead set to 20.
quiz.a: K<sub>c</sub> = 40/(2 × 10) = 2. If K<sub>c</sub> = 20, the low-frequency gain becomes 20 × 2 × 10 = 400, ten times too large — the lag boost β has been counted twice.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, lag-lead ideas appear in PID autotuners, where a lag is used for integral action and a lead for derivative action; the same phase and gain trade-off appears. Search for 'lead-lag compensator Bode design', 'PID phase margin', and 'loop shaping'. Modern robust control generalizes this to H∞ loop shaping, where weights play the role of the lag and lead sections.
